# Instructor Guide — Part 3 (10/17, Hour 3): Team Report-Outs, Synthesis, and What's Next {#sec-mod3-part3-guide}

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How to use this guide"}
This is a facilitation guide for the instructor, not student-facing reading. It pairs with the slide deck `mod3_part3_slides.qmd`. This hour closes out both the case discussion and Module 3 as a whole, then previews Module 4. Per the course outline, Project Oxygen's applied work *is* this team-based evaluation of the evidence and proposed improvements, this hour's report-outs and synthesis satisfy that requirement; there is no separate written case deliverable unless you choose to assign one.
:::

## Session Objectives

By the end of this period, students should be able to:

1. Compare their team's reasoning about Project Oxygen against other teams' reasoning, surfacing disagreement and consensus.
2. Articulate, as a class, a short list of concrete improvements that would strengthen the causal claim that "managers matter."
3. Summarize how Module 3's toolkit (comparisons, causation checklist) fits into the full analytics decision cycle, and what's coming next in Module 4.

| Time | Segment | Format |
|---|---|---|
| 0:00–0:05 | Re-entry: quick reminder of the worksheet | Instructor-led |
| 0:05–0:35 | Team report-outs | Whole-class discussion |

## Detailed Run of Show

### Re-entry: Quick Reminder of the Worksheet (5 min)

Briefly restate the six worksheet prompts from Part 2 so the room is oriented before report-outs begin.

### Team Report-Outs (30 min)

Call on each team's spokesperson for their assigned item (roughly 3&ndash;4 minutes per team, depending on class size). As each team reports, note points of **agreement and disagreement** on the board, especially:

- Which confounders came up more than once (a strong signal they're genuinely important, not idiosyncratic).
- Whether teams' proposed "stronger designs" actually specified who gets randomly assigned to what, or stayed vague, this is worth calling out live if it happens.
- Whether teams' final verdicts differed, and why. Disagreement here is a feature, not a problem, this is exactly the kind of judgment call real people-analytics teams have to make.

### Synthesis: The Class's Consolidated Position (15 min)

Pull the board's contents into a short, class-generated list:

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="A representative synthesis (yours will vary by class)"}
- **Strongest confounders identified:** team quality/resources at time of manager assignment; reverse causation (good teams make managers look good); self-selection into management roles.
- **Most concrete stronger design proposed:** randomly assign manager-behavior coaching (based on the eight identified attributes) to a subset of managers, holding a comparable group back as a control, then compare team outcomes after a fixed period.
- **Class verdict:** the evidence is suggestive and internally consistent across several outcomes, but remains observational; a randomized coaching rollout, even a modest pilot, would meaningfully strengthen the causal claim.
:::

Explicitly tie this back to the analytics decision cycle: the class has just done "quantify uncertainty" and a first pass at "recommend an action" (propose a stronger design), using real, messy business evidence rather than a clean textbook dataset.

### Module 3 Wrap-Up and Module 4 Preview (10 min)

Close out Module 3 by naming what it added to the toolkit: one-sample and two-sample comparisons, paired designs, ANOVA and Tukey's HSD, and, critically, the judgment to ask whether a statistically supported comparison actually supports a *causal* claim. Preview Module 4 (11/13): the course moves from *comparing groups* to *modeling relationships*, regression, the start of the **build a model** step of the decision cycle, letting us predict one variable from another rather than just comparing groups to each other.
